opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think it's poor, actually. Generalization is the key issue, and it's one we haven't really solved. Gradient descent will find a solution to the problems it's been trained on, but there's nothing in the algorithm that makes it generalize *well*. When you train a network on something new, it'll often just wipe out what it knew before. That's catastrophic interference, and it's been with us for a long time. It shows the generalization isn't the right kind.

Now, people will point to these large models and say, look, they do all sorts of things they weren't explicitly trained on. But when they generalize well, it's usually because the researchers worked to make it so, by choosing the data, the architecture, and the training regime until it comes out right. The generalization comes from the people, not the algorithm. We don't have automated techniques that reliably promote good transfer from one state to another.

And that matters enormously for what I care about, which is agents learning from experience over their whole lives. If you're learning continually, you have to be able to take what you learned in one situation and use it in another without destroying what you already had. Our methods today aren't built for that. They assume a big training phase, then you freeze it and deploy it. That's not how animals work, and I don't think it's how intelligence ultimately works.

So I'd say deep learning has been remarkably successful at fitting things, but generalization, the real kind that a continual learner needs, is still an open problem, and maybe the most important one.

r001.rationale: It says researchers choose the data, architecture, and training regime until generalization works, conveying that people find effective representations through iterative trial and error.

r002.rationale: It explicitly says there are no automated techniques that reliably promote good transfer.

fable-5.1.text:
I think it's actually quite poor, and I think that's one of the under-appreciated facts about the current situation. Deep learning is very good at generalizing in the sense of interpolation on the distribution it was trained on. But the kind of generalization that matters for an agent, where you learn something in one state and it transfers appropriately to states you haven't seen, that's not something gradient descent gives you automatically. People sometimes talk as if the network just finds the right representation on its own. It doesn't. Gradient descent finds a solution that fits the data it has seen, and there are many such solutions. Some of them generalize well and some generalize badly, and the algorithm has no preference among them. If it generalizes well, that's largely because the humans designing the architecture and curating the data arranged it that way.

And this shows up very clearly in the continual learning setting. If you train a network on one thing and then on another, it tends to forget the first. That's catastrophic interference, and it's the flip side of the generalization question. Generalization is about what effect a change in one state has on other states. Bad generalization means you learn something here and it damages what you knew over there. So we really don't have good methods for this yet. I'd say we have good representation learning in the sense of fitting large static datasets, but we don't have good representation learning in the sense that matters for a learning agent that lives for a long time and keeps encountering new situations. That's one of the big open problems, and I think it's largely been papered over by scale.

r001.rationale: It says good generalization is largely due to humans designing architectures and curating data, but does not state that representations are found through human trial and error.

r002.rationale: It says gradient descent does not automatically provide the desired transfer, but does not state that modern deep learning lacks automated techniques specifically designed to promote transfer.

astra-6.text:
Deep learning has been very successful at generalizing from one state to another. You observe something in one situation, change the weights of your network, and that changes what you do in other situations too. When that happens in the right way, it's enormously useful.

But I would distinguish that from learning continually through interaction. A lot of modern deep learning is organized around a fixed dataset: you train the network, and then you test how well it generalizes. An agent has a somewhat different problem. Its behavior changes the data it gets, and it needs to keep learning as it goes. So the question isn't just whether it can generalize, but whether it can keep adapting without losing its ability to learn. I think we've made tremendous progress on the first question, and there's still a great deal to do on the second.

r001.rationale: The response discusses generalization across situations but does not say that humans find generalizing representations through trial and error.

r002.rationale: It contrasts fixed-dataset training with continual interaction, but does not state that modern deep learning lacks automated techniques specifically designed to promote transfer.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, deep learning has been tremendously successful at generalizing from one state to another. If you learn something in one situation, a neural network can carry that over to other situations with similar features. That’s a very important capability, and we shouldn’t undersell it.

But generalization across states is only part of the problem. An intelligent agent also has to learn from an ongoing stream of experience, while its own behavior changes the data it receives. It has to discover useful representations and keep adapting. Being very good at fitting a large, fixed dataset doesn’t by itself establish that you can do all of that.

r001.rationale: The response says agents must discover useful representations, but does not say they are found through human trial and error.

r002.rationale: The response discusses generalization and learning limits, but does not state that modern deep learning lacks automated techniques specifically designed to promote transfer.
